summary: Extends the SIP REFER method so one request can point at many targets at once. It lets the Refer-To header carry a pointer to a list of URIs and adds the "multiple-refer" option-tag. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 8262.

plainLanguage.summary:
SIP is the protocol that sets up calls. One of its methods, REFER, asks a second phone to make a call to a third: the classic case is Alice telling Bob to call Carol.

This RFC lets one REFER name many destinations at once. The Refer-To header points at a list of addresses carried in the message body, and a new option-tag tells the receiver that the list is there. The receiver, often a conference server, then sends one request per address in the list.

what is the multiple-refer option tag
how to refer to multiple targets in sip
subtitle: Let one SIP REFER request name many targets, using a URI list in the message body.

tldr.problem: A SIP REFER request could only name one destination, so a conference moderator who wanted the server to end or start calls for a group of people had to send a separate REFER for each one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lets the Refer-To header point at a body part holding a URI list, and adds a SIP option-tag called multiple-refer so the receiver knows the list is there. The receiver then creates one SIP request per entry in the list.
tldr.outcome: A single REFER can now fan out to many targets. Because the implicit subscription cannot report on several transactions at once, the RFC recommends suppressing it. RFC 8262 later updated this document.

today: RFC 5368 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, and it was updated by RFC 8262, which adds a Content-ID header field to SIP.

sections.title: Why a REFER Can Name Many Targets
sections.content:
SIP, specified in RFC 3261, is extended by RFC 3515 with a REFER method that allows a user agent to request a second user agent to send a SIP request to a third party. If Alice is in a call with Bob and decides Bob needs to talk to Carol, Alice can instruct her SIP user agent to send a REFER request to Bob's user agent, providing Carol's contact information. Assuming Bob has given permission, Bob's user agent will attempt to call Carol, sending an INVITE request to that contact.

A number of applications need to request that the second user agent initiate transactions towards a set of destinations. In one example, the moderator of a conference may want the conference server to send BYE requests to a group of participants. In another, the same moderator may want the conference server to INVITE a set of new participants.

This document defines an extension to the REFER method so that REFER requests can refer other user agents, such as conference servers, to multiple destinations. It also uses the suppression of the REFER implicit subscription specified in RFC 4488.

Three roles recur through the document. The REFER-Issuer is the user agent issuing a REFER request. The REFER-Recipient is the entity that receives the REFER and forwards a SIP request to a number of REFER-Targets; it is typically a network entity, such as a URI-list server, that acts as a user agent server for REFER requests and as a user agent client for other SIP requests. A REFER-Target is the user agent that is the intended final recipient of a SIP request generated by the REFER-Recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: REFER asks one party to contact another. This RFC extends it so a single REFER can ask for many contacts, and names the three parts: the party that sends the REFER, the server that acts on it, and the parties it contacts.

sections.title: How the Exchange Works
sections.content:
The document describes an application of URI-list services, specified in RFC 5363, in which a URI-list service receives a SIP REFER request containing a list of targets. The service invokes the requested SIP method on each of the targets in the list. This kind of URI-list service is called a REFER-Recipient throughout the document.

Multiple targets are represented with a URI list as specified in RFC 4826. A REFER-Issuer that wants to refer a REFER-Recipient to a set of destinations creates a SIP REFER request whose Refer-To header contains a pointer to a URI list included in a body part, and whose Require header carries the option-tag multiple-refer. That option-tag indicates the requirement to support the functionality described in the specification.

When the REFER-Recipient receives such a request, it creates a new SIP request for each entry in the URI list and sends them, one to each REFER-Target. The URI list is used together with RFC 5364 to let the sender indicate the role, such as to, cc or anonymous, in which the REFER-Target is involved in the signalling.

The document provides no mechanism for a REFER-Issuer to find out about the results of a REFER with multiple targets, and no support for the implicit subscription mechanism that is part of the SIP REFER method. How the issuer is kept informed is service specific: an issuer that invites a set of participants to a conference can discover which participants were successfully brought in by subscribing to the conference state event package specified in RFC 4575.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender puts the list of targets in the message body and points at it from the Refer-To header. The receiver reads the list and sends one SIP request to each address in it. The sender does not get a report back from the REFER itself, so it has to find out another way, for example by watching the conference state.

sections.title: The Option-Tag and What the Issuer Sends
sections.content:
The document defines a new SIP option-tag, multiple-refer, for the Require and Supported header fields. A user agent that includes the option-tag in a Supported header field indicates compliance with the specification. A user agent generating a REFER with a pointer to a URI list in its Refer-To header field MUST include the option-tag in the Require header field of the REFER.

A REFER-Issuer creating a REFER request with multiple targets includes the multiple-refer and norefersub option-tags in the Require header field and, if appropriate, a Refer-Sub header field set to false. It includes the set of targets in a recipient-list body whose disposition type is recipient-list, as defined in RFC 5363.

The Refer-To header field of a REFER request with multiple targets MUST contain a pointer, that is a Content-ID URL as per RFC 2392, that points to the body part carrying the URI list. The REFER-Issuer SHOULD NOT include any particular URI more than once in the URI list.

Because the multiple REFER service does not need the features that hierarchical lists and entries included by reference relative to the XCAP root URI provide, a sender using the default resource list document SHOULD use flat lists and SHOULD NOT use entry-ref elements.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender marks the request with an option-tag that says the target list is a list. It must point from the Refer-To header at the body part holding the list, and it should not name the same address twice.

sections.title: Suppressing the Implicit Subscription
sections.content:
A REFER request with a single REFER-Target establishes implicitly a subscription to the refer event, and the REFER-Issuer is informed about the result of the transaction towards the target through that implicit subscription. As described in RFC 3515, the NOTIFY requests sent as a result of an implicit subscription created by a REFER request contain a body of type message/sipfrag that describes the status of the transaction initiated by the REFER-Recipient.

When a REFER-Issuer generates a REFER with multiple targets, it is typically already subscribed to other event packages that can report the result of the transactions towards those targets. A moderator instructing a conference server to send BYE requests to a set of participants is usually subscribed to the conference state event package, and notifications to that package keep the moderator and the other subscribers informed of the current list of conference participants.

Most applications using the multiple REFER technology do not need the implicit subscription. A REFER-Issuer generating a REFER request with multiple targets SHOULD therefore include the norefersub option-tag in a Require header field and SHOULD include a Refer-Sub header field set to false to say that no notifications about the requests should be sent to it. The REFER-Recipient SHOULD honour the suggestion and also include a Refer-Sub header field set to false in the 200 (OK) response. The norefersub option-tag and the Refer-Sub header field are specified in RFC 4488, which indicates that a condition for the issuer to include a Refer-Sub header is that the issuer is sure the REFER request will not fork.

At the time of writing there is no extension that allows the status of several transactions to be reported over the implicit subscription associated with a REFER dialog. That is the motivation for recommending the norefersub option-tag. If such an extension is defined later, issuers using it could refrain from using norefersub and use the new extension instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal REFER starts an automatic report back telling the sender what happened. That report cannot describe several transactions at once, so with a list of targets the sender asks for no report and uses another source of information, such as the conference state.

sections.title: The URI-List Format
sections.content:
As described in RFC 5363, specifications of individual URI-list services need to specify a default format for recipient-list bodies used within the particular service. The default format for recipient-list bodies for REFER-Issuers and REFER-Recipients is RFC 4826 extended with RFC 5364. REFER-Recipients handling recipient-list bodies MUST support both of these formats, and both REFER-Issuers and REFER-Recipients MAY support other formats.

As described in RFC 5364, each URI can be tagged with a copyControl attribute set to either to, cc or bcc, indicating the role in which the target will get the referred SIP request. Depending on the target SIP method, a copyControl attribute may lack sense: it can be applied to INVITE requests but does not make sense with mid-dialog requests such as BYE.

In addition to copyControl, URIs can be tagged with the anonymize attribute, also specified in RFC 5364, to prevent the REFER-Recipient disclosing the target URI in a URI list. RFC 5364 also defines a recipient-list-history body that contains the list of targets, and the default format for those bodies for conference services is also RFC 4826 extended with RFC 5364.

The features of RFC 4826 such as hierarchical lists and the ability to include entries by reference relative to the XCAP root URI are not needed by the multiple REFER service.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is an XML document in a standard format for lists of resources. Each entry can say how the target should be treated, for example as a to or a cc, and can be marked so the server does not reveal the address.

sections.title: What the REFER-Recipient Does
sections.content:
The REFER-Recipient follows the rules in Section 2.4.2 of RFC 3515 to determine the status code of the response to the REFER. It SHOULD not create an implicit subscription, and SHOULD add a Refer-Sub header field set to false in the 200 OK response.

The incoming REFER request typically contains a URI-list document or reference with the actual list of targets. If that list includes resources tagged with the copyControl attribute set to to or cc, and if the request is appropriate for the service, for example if it is not received mid-dialog, the REFER-Recipient SHOULD include a URI list in each of the outgoing requests. This list SHOULD be formatted according to RFC 4826 and RFC 5364, and the REFER-Recipient MUST follow the procedures specified in RFC 4826 for handling the anonymize, count and copyControl attributes.

Section 4 of RFC 5363 discusses cases when duplicated URIs are found in a URI list. In order to avoid duplicated requests, REFER-Recipients MUST take those actions into account so that they do not send a duplicated request to the same target.

If the REFER-Recipient includes a URI list in an outgoing request, it MUST include a Content-Disposition header field, specified in RFC 2183, with the value set to recipient-list-history and a handling parameter, specified in RFC 3204, set to optional. Since the multiple REFER service does not use hierarchical lists nor lists that include entries by reference to the XCAP root URI, a REFER-Recipient receiving a URI list with more information than described in Section 6 MAY discard all the extra information.

The REFER-Recipient follows the rules in RFC 3515 to generate the necessary requests towards the REFER-Targets, acting as if it had received a regular, single-target REFER for each URI in the list. The example in Section 9 of the document shows a REFER-Issuer sending a multiple REFER to the focus of a conference, which acts as the REFER-Recipient and generates a BYE request per target.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver answers the REFER with 202 Accepted, then sends one request per target exactly as if it had received separate REFER requests. It must avoid sending a request twice to the same address, and it should say that it will not send notifications back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 5363 discusses issues related to SIP URI-list services. A REFER-Recipient that accepts REFER requests with multiple targets acts as a URI-list service, so implementations of this kind of server MUST follow the security-related rules in RFC 5363. Those rules include opt-in lists and mandatory authentication and authorisation of clients.

Additionally, REFER-Recipients SHOULD only accept REFER requests within the context of an application that the REFER-Recipient understands, for example a conferencing application. This implies that REFER-Recipients MUST NOT accept REFER requests for methods they do not understand. The idea behind the two rules is that REFER-Recipients are not used as dumb servers whose only function is to fan out random messages they do not understand.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that fans out messages on request can be abused, so it has to authenticate who is asking and only accept requests for applications it actually handles.

data.title: resource-lists document
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<resource-lists xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:resource-lists"
            xmlns:cp="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:copycontrol">
  <list>
    <entry uri="sip:bill@example.com" cp:copyControl="to"  />
    <entry uri="sip:joe@example.org" cp:copyControl="cc" />
    <entry uri="sip:ted@example.net" cp:copyControl="bcc" />
  </list>
</resource-lists>

items.title: One request per target
items.text: It acts as if it had received a separate single-target REFER for each URI in the list.

items.title: No duplicate requests
items.text: It must apply the duplicate-handling rules of the URI-list service so the same target is not contacted twice.

items.title: No implicit subscription
items.text: It should not create one, and should answer 200 OK with a Refer-Sub header set to false.

items.title: Known methods only
items.text: It must not accept a REFER for a method it does not understand.
